web_evidence.title: A Common Life: The Wedding Story by Jan Karon | Excerpt
web_evidence.note: A sustained excerpt reprinted with Viking's permission narrates Father Timothy externally as he and gives direct access to his thoughts, establishing third-person narration throughout Chapter One.

web_evidence.title: A Common Life: The Wedding Story — Jan Karon — Google Books
web_evidence.note: The book preview independently displays sustained prose referring to Father Tim as he while rendering his perceptions and thoughts; its coverage remains within the opening chapter.

web_evidence.title: A Common Life by Jan Karon — Reading Guide
web_evidence.note: The publisher's whole-book guide describes scenes centered on Father Tim and other named residents, and Karon explains that she sometimes steps away to scenes at the Grill. This corroborates externally narrated, shifting focalization, although the guide does not explicitly use the term third person.

web_evidence.title: marching forth, with books | cakes, tea and dreams
web_evidence.note: A reader of the full series says this volume switches back and forth among multiple characters' perspectives. This clarifies the rotating focalization but does not by itself identify grammatical narrative person.

web_evidence.title: A Common Life Chapter Summary | Jan Karon
web_evidence.note: Chapter-by-chapter summaries report interior attention shifting among Father Tim, Uncle Billy, Dooley, Hope, and others through the final chapters. Because summary grammar is not narrative-person evidence, this was used only to investigate structure.

person_note: The controlling narrator is nonparticipating and uses third person, with close access to Father Tim in the authorized opening. Whole-book structural sources indicate that focalization later shifts among several Mitford residents; this is rotating third-person perspective, not ALTERNATING narrative person. The Goodreads quotes are mostly aphorisms, advice, or character prayers, and the lone possible narrative fragment is too clipped to diagnose person. No credible evidence of first- or second-person base sections was found. Confidence is medium because sustained primary prose was available only for the opening and the input quotes do not independently corroborate the classification.
